title: Taoism
summary: Taoism is one of the main traditions of Chinese thought, linked with the names of Laozi (the Tao Te Ching) and Zhuangzi. At its center is the Tao, “the Way”: a nameless natural order through which everything arises, changes and returns to its source. Wisdom, for the Taoists, lies in not forcing the nature of things but moving along with it, like water.
onEmotions: Taoists see feelings as part of life’s natural movement — like changes in the weather or the turning of the seasons: joy and sadness, rise and fall pass into one another, like yin and yang. Zhuangzi wrote that joy and anger, sorrow and delight, worry and regret follow one another day and night, and no one knows where they spring from. The trouble isn’t the feelings, but that we freeze up: we cling to one, wage war on another, judge ourselves by other people’s measures. The Taoist ideal is wu wei, “non-action” — that is, action without force or needless effort: letting a feeling flow, without inflating it or suppressing it.

anxiety.text: Anxiety makes sense: the mind is trying to foresee everything so as not to miss anything. Taoism looks at this state with gentle sympathy. Zhuangzi described how people, day and night, grapple with everything they meet, wearing out their hearts with small and large worries — and how this wears life away. The Taoist answer isn’t even more control, but wu wei, non-action: not doing nothing, but letting go of needless, forceful effort. Water doesn’t plan its path in advance, yet it always finds its way. Zhuangzi also spoke of the “fasting of the heart” — a quiet state in which you listen not only with the mind but with your whole being, becoming empty and open, like an empty room that light comes into. You can accept anxiety as a wave — and let it pass through without clinging.
anxiety.practice: Sit for a minute, listening to the sounds around you without naming them. Imagine that your heart is an empty, bright room that anxiety can pass right through.

fear.text: Fear is a natural part of life, and the Taoists didn’t consider it a disgrace. But they noticed that fear often arises when we hold on to one side of life and dread the other: we cling to success and fear failure, cling to health and fear illness. The Tao Te Ching says that opposites give birth to each other: difficult and easy, long and short, high and low. From a Taoist point of view, the world is constant transformation, and every change holds not only a threat but a possibility. Zhuangzi tells of a swimmer who swam unharmed in the churning water beneath a waterfall: he went down with the whirlpool and came up with it, never setting himself against the water. You can meet fear the same way — not freezing in resistance, but moving along with what is happening, step by step.
fear.practice: Ask yourself: what exactly am I resisting right now? What would one step “with the current,” rather than against it, look like?

sadness.text: Sadness is as natural as autumn or dusk, and Taoism sees no reason to be ashamed of it. In the Taoist picture of the world everything moves in cycles: a rise is followed by a fall, light by shadow, yang passes into yin so as to become yang again. Sadness is a yin time: quiet, slow, turned inward. The Tao Te Ching says that turning back into its opposite is the movement of the Tao, and softness and weakness are how it works. You could say sadness isn’t a malfunction but one of the natural rhythms, like an ebb tide. From a Taoist point of view, there’s no need to force yourself into cheerfulness; you can let this time be. Just as winter doesn’t hinder spring but prepares for it, sadness can turn out to be a time of quietly gathering strength within.
sadness.practice: Imagine what season or time of day it is inside you right now. What does this time need — rest, warmth, quiet? Give yourself a little of it.

grief.text: Loss is a great pain, and Taoism doesn’t deny it. There is a well-known story in the Zhuangzi: when Zhuangzi’s wife died, his friend Huizi found him sitting on the ground, drumming on a basin and singing. To his indignant friend Zhuangzi replied that at first, of course, he had grieved like anyone. But then he reflected: once she had not existed; then out of a dim chaos came breath, qi; from it a form; from the form, life; now another transformation had taken place, like the passing of spring, summer, autumn and winter. This story doesn’t suggest you stop grieving — Zhuangzi himself grieved. It shows that in time the pain can join with a sense of the great cycle of which the loved one was a part. You can grieve and at the same time feel that your bond with them has not vanished from the world.
grief.practice: If you feel like it, step outside and look at something living — a tree, the sky. Silently tell the one you lost that you remember them.

loneliness.text: Loneliness is painful, and there’s nothing strange about longing for closeness. Taoism, though, also sees a bright side to solitude. Zhuangzi wrote of “free and easy wandering” — a state in which the spirit isn’t tied to others’ approval and can soar far and wide, like the enormous bird Peng in his parable. Taoist hermits went off into the mountains not out of resentment toward people, but to hear the silence and feel their connection with “the ten thousand things” — the Chinese name for all the multiplicity of the world. From a Taoist point of view, you could say you are never completely cut off: you are part of the same nature as the trees, the wind, other people. Loneliness can become a time when this connection is felt more quietly, but more deeply. And longing for people is also a natural movement you can follow.
loneliness.practice: Look out the window or step outside for five minutes and find something living with your eyes. Say to yourself: “I am part of this too.”

anger.text: Anger is a powerful energy, and there’s nothing unnatural about it. Taoism, however, pays attention to how it works. The Tao Te Ching keeps returning to the image of water: it is the softest thing in the world, yet it wears away the hardest stone. Strength, for Laozi, lies not in rigidity but in flexibility: what is hard and unbending is closer to death, and what is soft and supple is closer to life, like a young tree that bends in the wind but doesn’t break. From a Taoist point of view, anger frozen into rigid opposition exhausts you first of all. But its energy can be directed differently — like water, which doesn’t argue with a stone but flows around it and still reaches its goal. You can admit “I’m angry” — and choose a path that is gentle but persistent.
anger.practice: Ask yourself: what do I actually want to achieve in this situation? What would a path “like water” look like — gentle, but unrelenting?

quote.text: In the world there is nothing more submissive and weak than water. Yet for attacking that which is hard and strong nothing can surpass it.
quote.author: Laozi
quote.source: Tao Te Ching, 78 (trans. D. C. Lau)

shame.text: Shame is often born of measuring yourself against standards: how you ought to be, what is proper, what counts as success. Taoism treats such standards with deep distrust. Laozi wrote that when everyone recognizes beauty as beautiful, ugliness appears: judgments give birth to their doubles. Zhuangzi collected stories of people with disabilities, strange looks or low standing who were wise and drew others to them. One of his favorite parables is about an old, crooked tree that a carpenter deemed useless: precisely for that reason it wasn’t cut down, and it grew enormous. From a Taoist point of view, what embarrasses you may turn out to be part of your true nature — pu, “the uncarved block,” a simplicity that doesn’t need to be trimmed to fit someone else’s pattern.
shame.practice: Name the standard by which you are shaming yourself right now. Ask: whose standard is it? Who would I be without it?

guilt.text: Guilt tells you that the consequences of your actions matter to you, and that’s important. Taoism says little about guilt in our usual sense — it is more interested in naturalness than in moral rules. Laozi even remarked that loud talk of benevolence and righteousness appears when the great Way has been lost — living, spontaneous kindness. From a Taoist point of view, you could say guilt is useful as long as it brings you back to that simple kindness, and harmful when it turns into endless self-condemnation. The Tao Te Ching asks: who can, by being still, make muddy water clear? Water that is no longer stirred clears by itself. You can admit your mistake, set right what is possible, and let the muddy water settle.
guilt.practice: Ask yourself: what can I set right? Do it, or write it down. Then sit for a minute, imagining the muddy water in a vessel slowly becoming clear.

envy.text: Envy is a natural echo of comparison, and you don’t need to be ashamed of it. Taoism, however, looks at comparison itself with suspicion. The Tao Te Ching says there is no greater misfortune than not knowing when enough is enough, and that one who knows contentment is always content. This isn’t about resigning yourself to want, but about inner freedom: as long as your happiness is measured by other people’s successes, it is always in their hands. Zhuangzi tells of creatures that envy one another in a circle: the one-legged creature envies the millipede, the millipede envies the snake, the snake envies the wind, the wind envies the eye, the eye envies the heart. Each has its own makeup and its own path. From a Taoist point of view, you can take envy as a reminder to return to your own nature — and to what you already have.
envy.practice: Name one quality or circumstance of yours that belongs to your path alone. What is valuable in it that can’t be seen from outside?

quote.text: There is no disaster greater than not being content; there is no misfortune greater than being covetous. Hence in being content, one will always have enough.
quote.author: Laozi
quote.source: Tao Te Ching, 46 (trans. D. C. Lau)

emptiness.text: A sense of emptiness and apathy can be heavy, and it deserves gentle care. Taoism can offer an unexpected view: in its language, emptiness is not only a lack but also a source of possibility. Laozi gives examples: a wheel works thanks to the emptiness at its hub, a jug thanks to the emptiness inside, a room thanks to the openings of its windows and doors. Usefulness arises where there is space. From a Taoist point of view, you could say that your present emptiness isn’t necessarily an ending, but perhaps a cleared space in which something new hasn’t appeared yet. There’s no need to fill it in a hurry. The Taoists spoke of xu — the emptiness, the openness of the heart in which calm is born. You can simply stay in this state, looking after your body and your rest, and let the new come in its own time.
emptiness.practice: Look at any vessel nearby — a cup, a bowl — and notice: it is useful thanks to its emptiness. Ask yourself: what might space be clearing in me for?

quote.text: Thirty spokes share one hub. Adapt the nothing therein to the purpose in hand, and you will have the use of the cart.
quote.author: Laozi
quote.source: Tao Te Ching, 11 (trans. D. C. Lau)

confusion.text: Confusion is an honest state, when the old answers no longer fit. Strange as it may seem, Taoism values this “not-knowing.” The opening lines of the Tao Te Ching say that what matters most doesn’t fit into ready-made formulas. Zhuangzi told how he once dreamed he was a butterfly, fluttering about carefree — and on waking he couldn’t tell whether it was Zhuangzi who had dreamed of being a butterfly, or a butterfly now dreaming it was Zhuangzi. This parable teaches lightness toward uncertainty. From a Taoist point of view, you don’t have to understand everything right away. You can move like water: without knowing the whole map, but sensing the nearest slope of the ground. Clarity often comes by itself once you stop hurrying it.
confusion.practice: Ask yourself not “what is right overall,” but “in which direction is it easiest for me to take one next step?” Write that step down.

quote.text: The way that can be spoken of is not the constant way.
quote.author: Laozi
quote.source: Tao Te Ching, 1 (trans. D. C. Lau)

fatigue.text: Tiredness and burnout are a sign that you’ve been going against your own current for a long time. Taoism understands this very well. Zhuangzi has a parable about Cook Ding, who carved up an ox so easily it was as if he were dancing: in nineteen years his knife never grew dull. The secret was that he didn’t hack at random, but followed the natural gaps and joints, finding the path of least resistance. Ordinary cooks change their knife every month, because they hack at bone. From a Taoist point of view, burnout is when we have been “hacking at bone” for too long: spending our strength on struggle rather than on moving along natural lines. Wu wei, non-action, isn’t laziness but the art of acting without needless force against yourself. Rest and a return to your own rhythm are part of the Way too.
fatigue.practice: Recall what has cost you the most strain over the last few days. Is there a “gap” there — an easier way, like Cook Ding’s?

boredom.text: Boredom can be oppressive: the world seems flat and time empty. From a Taoist point of view, you could say boredom sometimes comes from expecting that life should entertain us with something special. Zhuangzi and his friend Huizi were once strolling on a bridge over a river. Zhuangzi remarked how freely the little fish were swimming — that is the joy of fish. His friend objected: you’re not a fish, so how do you know what the fish enjoy? The argument was philosophical, but the scene itself shows the Taoist attention to the simple: to fish, water, the moment. For a Taoist, the ordinary holds inexhaustible variety — “the ten thousand things,” constantly changing. You can accept boredom as a pause in which the eye learns to see anew, without hurry.
boredom.practice: Choose one ordinary thing nearby — a leaf, a cloud, the steam over a cup — and watch it for a minute, the way Zhuangzi watched the fish.

joy.text: Joy is a natural expression of life, and Taoism welcomes it, especially when it is simple and unforced. Zhuangzi is one of the most cheerful philosophers in history: his book is full of jokes, paradoxes, odd characters and play. Its first chapter is called “Free and Easy Wandering” — about the lightness of a spirit not bound by rules or by concern for gain. In the Taoist sense, joy is especially pure when it is ziran — “so of itself,” natural, not squeezed out of yourself and not dependent on anyone’s approval. At the same time, the Taoists remembered that everything turns into its opposite, and they didn’t try to hold on to joy forever. That is exactly why you can live it fully: like a wind that comes and goes, leaving freshness behind.
joy.practice: Remember when today you were glad for no particular reason, or over something small. Let yourself feel it again for a few breaths.

love.text: Love and tenderness are among the most natural feelings, and in Taoism they are close to the very nature of the Way. Laozi named the “three treasures” he holds dear, and the first of them is ci, translated as love, compassion or motherly care. He said that true courage is born from this gentle love. In the Tao Te Ching the Tao is often described in motherly images — as the mother of all under heaven, who gives birth to and nourishes everything while possessing nothing. From a Taoist point of view, the deepest love is like this: it gives life without claiming, cares without controlling. You can take the tenderness you feel as an expression of this natural power — soft, but very strong.
love.practice: Think of someone you feel tenderness for. How could you show them care in a light way — without control or expectations?

gratitude.text: Gratitude is a warm feeling of connection with what sustains your life. Taoist texts say little about gratitude as a moral duty, but from a Taoist point of view you could say it grows naturally out of seeing the Tao. The Tao Te Ching describes the Way as what gives birth to and nourishes everything, asking nothing in return and claiming no credit. Gratitude in this sense isn’t a reckoning of who owes whom, but wonder at the world’s generosity: air, water, light, the people nearby. Laozi wrote that one who knows contentment is rich. Gratitude helps you accept life as it is, noticing that even on hard days much goes on giving itself unconditionally.
gratitude.practice: Name three things that sustained your life today without asking anything in return — for example, air, light or someone’s smile.

hope.text: Hope helps us get through hard times, and Taoism gives it a special kind of support — not a promise that everything will be fine, but an understanding of how change works. The Tao Te Ching says that misfortune and good fortune are intertwined and pass into one another. There is also a well-known parable from the Huainanzi: an old man living near the frontier lost his horse — the neighbors commiserated, but he calmly asked how they knew this wasn’t for the good. The horse came back, bringing a fine stallion with it, and the story kept turning first one way, then the other. From a Taoist point of view, your present situation isn’t a final verdict. Hope here isn’t clinging to a particular outcome but openness: everything flows, and every situation already holds the seeds of something new.
hope.practice: Recall a time in the past when what seemed like a failure later turned into something important. What might that say about your present situation?

quote.text: It is on disaster that good fortune perches; it is beneath good fortune that disaster crouches.
quote.author: Laozi
quote.source: Tao Te Ching, 58 (trans. D. C. Lau)

nostalgia.text: Nostalgia is a tender longing for what has gone, and it reflects what is truly dear to you. Taoism sees this feeling as a natural response to the world’s main law — constant transformation. Zhuangzi spoke of ceaseless change, in which things pass into one another, and taught us to meet it without reproach. Laozi wrote of “returning to the root”: all the multiplicity of life ultimately returns to its source, and he called this return stillness. From a Taoist point of view, you could say nostalgia is a longing for the root, for that state of simplicity and wholeness we once felt. To touch it, you don’t have to bring back the past: the root is always here, in the quiet and simplicity of the present moment.
nostalgia.practice: Recall what you miss from the past and name it in one word — “simplicity,” “warmth,” “freedom.” Where in your present life could you find even a little of it?

craving.text: A craving — a sharp “I want it now” — can be as powerful as a current, and there’s no need to be ashamed of it. The Taoists didn’t condemn desires, but they looked closely at how they work. Laozi noticed that chasing ever stronger sensations doesn’t satisfy but dulls the senses: the more insistently we chase a stimulus, the less it gives. He saw the way out not in struggle but in pu — simplicity, the image of the uncarved block, the natural state before all the add-ons. You could say the Taoist approach to a wave of craving is wu wei, non-action: neither rushing into battle nor giving in, but letting the wave rise and pass, the way wind passes through bamboo. In the Taoist picture, everything that reaches its limit turns back — and so does a craving.
craving.practice: When a craving comes, imagine yourself as the shore and it as a wave. For a few minutes just watch it rise and recede, without jumping into the water.

addiction.text: Addiction isn’t a moral failure, but a deep rut that life slides back into again and again. The Taoists spoke a great deal about how life’s natural movement can freeze. Zhuangzi told of Cook Ding, who carved an ox so easily that his knife stayed sharp for nineteen years: he didn’t hack his way through but found the natural gaps between the joints. One thought can be drawn from this image: the way out of the circle is rarely found through force and a sudden lunge — more often through a patient search for “gaps,” places where you can pass more gently. Laozi valued water, which slowly but steadily changes stone. Taoism also speaks of “returning to the root” — to the simple and natural. This is a path of small steps, and every one of them counts.
addiction.practice: Notice one “gap” in your day — a moment when the circle loosens even a little. What is happening around you and inside you then?

hangover.text: The morning after — a heavy body, anxiety, shame, fragments of yesterday. Many people know this state, and it deserves gentleness, not a verdict. The Taoists saw life as an alternation of yin and yang: a rise is followed by a fall, noise by quiet, excess by depletion. From this angle, you could say a hard morning is a pendulum swinging back, not proof of your worthlessness. Taoist wisdom here is not to put yourself on trial, but to return to the simple: quiet, rest, slow breathing. Laozi called this “returning to the root.” Going over yesterday can wait until your head is clearer — then you’ll see what really needs attention and what was only morning anxiety.
hangover.practice: Allow yourself a few minutes of not deciding anything about yesterday. Just sit, feeling the support beneath you and your slow breathing.

euphoria.text: A burst of euphoria is bright, and you can live it with joy. Taoism isn’t against highs: Zhuangzi is one of the most cheerful philosophers, and his “free and easy wandering” is full of lightness. But the Taoists saw that everything in the world moves in a circle: having reached its peak, any phenomenon begins to turn back. The Tao Te Ching says that returning, turning into the opposite, is the very movement of the Tao. Knowing this doesn’t spoil the high but makes it lighter: there’s no need to cling and try to hold on to the peak. You could say the Taoist sage never flies higher than they can calmly come down from. Enjoying the wave while remembering the shore — that is Taoist grace.
euphoria.practice: While you’re on the high, do something small and earthy: drink some tea, take a walk, feel your feet. Let the joy be — and let it have something to stand on.

crash.text: A sharp drop after a high can be disheartening: yesterday everything shone, today it’s gray. Taoism sees this not as a breakdown but as a natural rhythm. Yin and yang pass into each other like day and night, and the drop is as much a part of the cycle as the rise. Laozi wrote that what is hollow becomes full, and what is worn becomes new. After yang — bright, loud, active — comes yin: quiet, rest, recovery. If you don’t wage war on the drop, it becomes a time when strength gathers anew, like the earth in winter. The Taoist advice is not to drive yourself back up to the peak, but to let yourself stay in the lowland for a while. Water, Laozi reminds us, flows downward — and that is exactly why it is closest to the Tao.
crash.practice: Treat today as a yin day: choose one quiet, restoring activity and allow it to yourself without guilt.

panic.text: A wave of panic is truly frightening: your heart pounds, you can’t get enough air, it seems something irreparable is about to happen. It isn’t your fault that it came. The Tao Te Ching has a simple observation about the nature of storms: even heaven and earth can’t keep up a gale or a downpour for long. You could say the wave inside a person is weather too: it rises and recedes. A wave of panic usually peaks and subsides within a few minutes. The Taoist image here is wu wei: not fighting the wave with all your might, since struggle often spurs it on, but becoming like water, which rides out a storm without breaking. You can hold on to something simple and steady while the wave passes.
panic.practice: Press your feet into the floor like roots and take a few breaths where the exhale is longer than the inhale. Silently name five things you can see around you.

quote.text: A gusty wind cannot last all morning, and a sudden downpour cannot last all day.
quote.author: Laozi
quote.source: Tao Te Ching, 23 (trans. D. C. Lau)

dread.text: Existential dread — “what’s the point of it all,” the thought of our finitude — is a very ancient experience, and there is no weakness in it. The Taoists looked into the same abyss, but saw in it not emptiness but a great movement. Zhuangzi described the world as a ceaseless “transformation of things”: everything arises from the Tao and returns to it, like the seasons. He also insisted that our small mind cannot grasp the whole — and that this is not a tragedy but a relief: you don’t need to know the answer to “what is it all for” in order to live. Meaning in Taoism isn’t a goal somewhere ahead, but the very flow of life: breath, the turning of the seasons, a conversation with a friend. Instead of the question of meaning, you can for a while trust the movement you are part of.
dread.practice: Go to the window or step outside, and for a minute watch something moving — clouds, leaves, people. Feel that you are part of this movement.

fomo.text: The feeling that everyone else is living more interesting lives and you’re not where you should be is exhausting — and very common. Zhuangzi would answer with a parable. In the first chapter of his book the enormous bird Peng rises ninety thousand li, and a cicada and a little dove laugh: why go so far, when we can barely make it to the nearest tree and that’s enough for us? Zhuangzi shows that each has its own scale and its own measure. Someone else’s life, seen in the feed, is no yardstick for yours. Laozi wrote that one who knows contentment is rich — meaning the ability to feel: this is enough for me. You could say the Taoist sage doesn’t run off to where “the important things are happening”: the important things happen wherever the sage is.
fomo.practice: Ask yourself: “What measure is mine?” Name one thing in today that is truly enough for you.

sleepless.text: Thoughts at three in the morning circle like leaves in a whirlpool, and they are hard to shake off. Very many people know this. The Taoists would say that night is a yin time, a time of rest and darkness, while the mind sometimes goes on living in the day, in yang: deciding, arguing, planning. Laozi asked: who can make muddy water clear? — and answered: if you leave it still, it will gradually clear. Night thoughts are the same muddy water: the more you stir it, the less you can see. The Taoist way is wu wei: not forcing yourself to fall asleep, but ceasing to struggle, letting thoughts drift past like clouds. Sleep, like everything natural, comes when it isn’t dragged.
sleepless.practice: Lying down, imagine that your thoughts are muddy water in a bowl. Don’t touch it; just watch the silt slowly settle to the bottom.

betrayal.text: Betrayal wounds where there was trust, and your pain is entirely natural. The Taoists saw plenty of human faithlessness: Zhuangzi lived in the Warring States period, full of intrigue and treachery. Their answer is neither to harden nor to pretend nothing happened. Laozi observed that what is alive is soft and supple, while what has withered is hard and brittle, and so he saw rigidity as the companion of decline and softness as the companion of life. Protecting yourself and keeping your distance is natural. But you don’t have to let betrayal turn your heart to stone. From a Taoist point of view, you could say that in time the wound can become a place where you understand people better, rather than a place of permanent defense.
betrayal.practice: Notice where in your body you are holding this pain — your shoulders, your jaw? Let that place soften, even for a few breaths.

jealousy.text: Jealousy is a mix of love, fear and insecurity, and there’s nothing shameful in it. Picture a Taoist image: water you try to squeeze in your fist runs through your fingers, while in an open palm it stays. From a Taoist point of view, you could say jealousy is an attempt to hold on to something that is by nature alive and free. Laozi wrote of the Tao that gives birth but does not claim, that nurtures but does not possess. Love in the Taoist spirit is like this: it nourishes but doesn’t hold by force. This doesn’t mean you should stay silent about your feelings. But you can notice where fear makes you clench your fist — and try to loosen it a little, leaning on your own inner steadiness.
jealousy.practice: Clench your fist for a few seconds, then slowly open your palm. Ask yourself: “What am I trying to hold on to — and what would help me feel safe?”

resentment.text: An old grudge is heavy, and it usually grew out of a real injustice. Taoism doesn’t demand that you forget it, but it notices how it keeps a person in the past. Zhuangzi tells the parable of the empty boat: if an empty boat drifts into your boat on the river, you won’t get angry, even if you’re hot-tempered; but if someone is sitting in it, you’ll start shouting. Zhuangzi doesn’t claim the one who hurt you is blameless. He invites you to see that a good part of the torment lies in the image of the other person that we carry with us for years. The Taoist way is to “empty your boat,” not to keep the old cargo on board. Letting go of a grudge doesn’t mean excusing it; it means freeing your own current.
resentment.practice: Imagine the grudge is cargo in your boat. Ask yourself: “What would change if I unloaded even part of it?” Write down the answer.

heartbreak.text: A breakup is a huge change, and the pain of a broken heart is entirely real. The Taoists saw life as a flow in which meetings and partings follow one another like the seasons. This doesn’t make the pain smaller, but it helps you not take it as proof that something is wrong with you. Laozi wrote that difficult and easy, high and low give rise to each other. You could say the depth of your sadness is the other side of the depth of your love. The Taoist way is not to hurry yourself or force the feeling: winter doesn’t turn into spring on command. But spring does come. While the yin time lasts, you can care for yourself gently, the way a gardener cares for sleeping earth.
heartbreak.practice: Ask yourself: “What care do I need in this ‘winter’?” Choose one gentle thing and do it for yourself today.

impostor.text: “Any minute now they’ll find me out” — this fear often comes to people who are actually trying hard and growing. Taoism looks at it in an unusual way: Laozi didn’t trust loud claims to knowledge at all. The sage in the Taoist picture is modest, senses the limits of their understanding and isn’t ashamed of them. From this angle, your feeling of “I don’t know everything” isn’t evidence against you but a sign of honesty. Zhuangzi tells of Wheelwright Bian, who explained to a duke: I feel my skill in my hands, and I can’t pass it on in words even to my son. Real skill lives in practice, not in titles and speeches. You’re not an impostor if you are learning your craft by doing it.
impostor.practice: Think of one skill that lives “in your hands” rather than in words. Write it down — this is your real experience.

quote.text: One who knows does not speak; one who speaks does not know.
quote.author: Laozi
quote.source: Tao Te Ching, 56 (trans. D. C. Lau)

self_hatred.text: If your inner critic is loud and merciless right now, you deserve gentleness, not agreement with its verdict. Taoism is especially far from self-flagellation. Zhuangzi loved “useless” characters: the crooked, gnarled tree that a carpenter judged worthless — and which, precisely for that reason, grew enormous and gave shade to many. He told of people with disabilities who were laughed at, yet in whom there was a remarkable fullness of de, inner power. The yardsticks your critic judges you by are often other people’s measures of “usefulness” and “correctness.” The Taoist thought is this: you don’t have to live up to them in order to have the right to be. Like a tree, you grow in your own shape.
self_hatred.practice: Write down one quality your critic calls a “flaw.” Ask yourself, as Zhuangzi did about the crooked tree: where might strength be hiding in it?

helplessness.text: Feeling powerless to change something is agonizing, and it’s important not to blame yourself for it. Taoism, in its own way, respects weakness. Laozi wrote that the soft and weak overcome the hard and strong, and that water, the most yielding thing in the world, wears away stone. This isn’t a consoling fairy tale: water doesn’t break a rock in a day; it acts constantly, little by little, finding the cracks. From a Taoist point of view, you could say helplessness before something large doesn’t cancel your “power of water” — a small but persistent presence. Wu wei isn’t passivity but action in harmony with circumstances: not beating your head against the wall, but looking for where it gives. And sometimes the best you can do is simply hold steady, like bamboo in the wind.
helplessness.practice: Ask yourself: “Where is there even a small crack here that water could seep through?” Name one gentle, almost unnoticeable action.

procrastination.text: “I can’t get started” is a state everyone knows, and it doesn’t make you a lazy person. Taoism invites you to look at it without forcing yourself. Laozi wrote that great things are made from small ones, and that the difficult begins with the easy. Often a task seems like a huge mountain, and the mind freezes before it. The Taoist move isn’t to storm the mountain, but to find the easiest place for the first step. Wu wei here isn’t idleness but the search for a beginning that doesn’t require breaking yourself. Water doesn’t argue with stone: it simply flows where the way is open. In the same way, a task begun with something small gradually gathers its current.
procrastination.practice: Find the easiest little piece of the task — so small it’s almost embarrassing to call it work. Do only that.

quote.text: The journey of a thousand miles starts from beneath one’s feet.
quote.author: Laozi
quote.source: Tao Te Ching, 64 (trans. D. C. Lau)

uprooted.text: Losing your home — a move, emigration — knocks the ground out from under your feet, and longing for what came before is entirely natural. The Taoist tradition knows about wandering: according to a legend retold by the historian Sima Qian, at the end of his life Laozi left the kingdom and went west, leaving his book behind at a frontier pass. The first chapter of the Zhuangzi is called “Free and Easy Wandering” — about a person who finds support not in a place but in harmony with the Tao. You could say the “root” Laozi speaks of isn’t only the land where you were born, but also a quiet center within, which you can return to anywhere. This doesn’t cancel the loss. But you aren’t an uprooted plant — you’re more like a seed looking for new soil, carrying everything that is yours within it.
uprooted.practice: Find one natural thing in your new place — a tree, a river, the sky above the rooftops — and spend a minute with it. It is the same as everywhere.

overload.text: An endless feed, notifications, noise — the mind gets tired of it, and that is a natural reaction to excess. Laozi described something similar two and a half thousand years ago, long before any screens: an excess of impressions doesn’t enrich the senses but dulls them. In the same chapter he writes that the sage cares for the belly and not for the eyes — that is, for what truly nourishes rather than what merely catches the eye. The Taoist answer to overload is pu, simplicity. You could say Taoist hygiene of the mind means returning from time to time to a few things: one sound, one taste, one task — and letting the rest go by.
overload.practice: Choose one simple sensation — the taste of tea, a sound outside the window — and stay with it alone for a minute, with the screen set aside.

quote.text: The five colours make man’s eyes blind; the five notes make his ears deaf; the five tastes injure his palate.
quote.author: Laozi
quote.source: Tao Te Ching, 12 (trans. D. C. Lau)

unreality.text: Sometimes the world or you yourself seem unreal, as if in a dream. It’s a strange, sometimes unsettling experience, and it can be talked about calmly. Taoism has a famous parable about exactly this: Zhuang Zhou dreamed he was a butterfly, fluttering about carefree; on waking, he couldn’t tell whether Zhou had dreamed he was a butterfly, or a butterfly was dreaming it was Zhou. Remarkably, this story isn’t frightening but light: Zhuangzi ends it with the thought of “the transformation of things.” Sleep and waking, butterfly and man are forms of one continuous flow. You could say Taoism doesn’t demand that you urgently settle what is “real.” And you can find support in the simple: here is your breath, here is the ground under your feet.
unreality.practice: Touch something with a pronounced texture — wood, fabric, stone — and describe the sensation to yourself. Let this touch be your bridge back to “here.”

awe.text: Awe before something vast or beautiful — mountains, the sky, the sea — is one of the most living experiences. Taoism, arguably, grew largely out of this feeling. The Tao, for Laozi, cannot be expressed in words; it is greater than any name, and it is natural to fall silent before it. Zhuangzi tells of the Lord of the Yellow River: in autumn, when the flood grew enormous, he became proud, but when he reached the Northern Sea and saw its boundlessness, he sighed in amazement. Awe is a moment when you, like that river, suddenly see the scale of the world. In the Taoist sense this isn’t a humiliation but the joy of belonging to the whole. Such a feeling doesn’t need explaining — it’s enough to stay in it for a while.
awe.practice: When you feel awe, stay silent for a minute, naming nothing. Just let yourself be a small part of something immense.

relief.text: Relief is a long-awaited breath out, and you can simply live it. Taoism sees in it the natural swing of a pendulum: tension has given way to release, yang to yin. Laozi compared the way of heaven to the stringing of a bow: what is raised too high is lowered, and what is low is raised. Relief shows how much strength was going into holding the tension. The Taoist advice is not to rush straight on to the next worry, but to let body and mind stay in the released state, the way a slackened bowstring rests. The wisdom of the Tao lies in alternation, not in endless effort. In the Taoist picture, rest isn’t a reward to be earned but just as legitimate a part of the cycle as work. Now is the time to let go.
relief.practice: Take a long breath out and let your shoulders drop. Stay in this “released” state for a few breaths, without hurrying to the next thing.

calm.text: Calm is a precious state, and for Taoism it is almost a homecoming. Laozi wrote: returning to the root is called stillness. Everything grows, blossoms, rustles — and then returns to its source, to silence. Taoist calm isn’t freezing up, but a depth like still water. Zhuangzi observed that people don’t look at their reflection in running water, but in still water: only a calm surface reflects clearly. Your calm makes you such a mirror — in it the world can be seen more distinctly. There’s no need to hold on to it by force: it’s enough to learn the way to it, so you can return again. The Taoists believed calm isn’t a rare gift but a natural state that everything tends to return to by itself, if only we stop getting in the way.
calm.practice: Stay in your calm for a minute, imagining yourself as still water. Notice what is reflected in it — which sounds, images, sensations.

inspiration.text: Inspiration is a living surge when you want to create, and Taoism values this state highly. Zhuangzi tells of craftsmen who worked as if not by their own will but in harmony with the nature of things. Before carving a stand for bells, Woodworker Qing fasted and stilled his mind until he forgot about rewards, praise and even his own body — and then he saw in the forest a tree in which the finished form was already hidden. You could say Taoist inspiration isn’t strained effort but ziran, naturalness: you stop getting in the way of what wants to be born. A Taoist’s advice to someone inspired is to follow this current, without hurrying to claim the result as your own.
inspiration.practice: Before you take up your idea, set aside thoughts of results and evaluations for a minute. Ask yourself, like Woodworker Qing: “What shape does this want to take?”

schadenfreude.text: Schadenfreude is a feeling people hide even from themselves, yet almost everyone knows it. Taoism would look at it through one of its favorite ideas — the relativity of good and bad fortune. The Huainanzi has a parable about an old man on the frontier whose horse ran away. The neighbors commiserated, but he asked: “How do you know this isn’t good luck?” The horse came back with a herd; then his son fell from a horse and was lamed; then, because of the limp, he wasn’t taken off to war. From a Taoist point of view, someone else’s failure is just one turn in the long alternation of yin and yang, and rejoicing in it is as premature as grieving over your own. You can notice schadenfreude as a sign that you’re measuring yourself against others — and gently return to your own current.
schadenfreude.practice: When you feel schadenfreude, say to yourself, like the old man on the frontier: “Who knows what this will lead to?” — and turn your attention to your own affairs.

contempt.text: Contempt divides the world into high and low — and Taoism treats such divisions with deep distrust. In the chapter “On the Equality of Things,” Zhuangzi shows that everyone judges from their own standpoint: sleeping in the damp is bad for a person but just right for an eel; people consider certain women beauties, but fish, on seeing them, dive into the depths. Who knows the true measure? From a Taoist point of view, contempt is a frozen judgment that mistakes a particular view for the final one. Laozi advised us to “blunt our sharpness” (chapter 56). This doesn’t mean approving of everything. But you can notice: what you despise is seen from a particular place, and from another place the world looks different. Contempt grows lighter when you step down from the pedestal.
contempt.practice: For a minute, try looking at the situation through the eyes of the person you feel contempt for: how does the world look from where they stand? You don’t have to agree — just look.

quote.text: He who knows others is clever; he who knows himself has discernment. He who overcomes others has force; he who overcomes himself is strong.
quote.author: Laozi
quote.source: Tao Te Ching, 33 (trans. D. C. Lau)

disgust.text: Disgust is one of the strongest responses of recoil, and it can be directed at people, situations and yourself. Taoism pays special attention to what we consider low and dirty. There is a famous dialogue in the Zhuangzi: Zhuangzi was asked where the Tao is. “Everywhere,” he answered. “Be more specific.” “In the ant.” “And lower still?” “In the weeds… in a potsherd… in piss and dung.” The questioner fell silent. From a Taoist point of view, the Way disdains nothing, and the division into clean and dirty is a human judgment. This doesn’t mean disgust is wrong: it protects. But it can soften if you remember that both what repels you and you yourself are part of one cycle. If the disgust is turned on yourself, Taoism would remind you: the Way doesn’t turn away from you either.
disgust.practice: Name what disgusts you and add: “And this, too, is part of the world.” Notice whether anything in your body shifts — even slightly.

revenge.text: The wish for revenge is understandable: you were hurt, and you want to restore the balance. Taoism speaks of balance too, but understands it differently. Laozi advised answering injury with virtue, de (chapter 63), and noted that after a great enmity some resentment always remains (chapter 79). This isn’t naivety: from a Taoist point of view, revenge is an attempt to bend the course of things by force, and violence breeds answering violence, spreading in circles like ripples on water. The image of water suggests something else too: water doesn’t take revenge on a stone, but flows around it and continues on its way. From a Taoist point of view, the strongest thing you can do with a hurt is not to let it define your path. You need your energy for your own current, not for punishing someone else.
revenge.practice: Imagine your hurt as a stone in a river. Ask yourself: how could the water flow around it and continue on? Write down one such step.

anger_at_loved.text: Anger at those close to you — a partner, parents, children — is especially painful, because shame quickly follows it. Taoism invites you to look at this through yin and yang: in every living bond there is attraction and repulsion, warmth and irritation, and one never comes without the other. The closer the person, the more often your currents collide. Zhuangzi told of a man crossing a river: if an empty boat bumps into his, he doesn’t get angry; if someone is sitting in it, he shouts at them (chapter 20). From a Taoist point of view, anger often concerns not the person themselves but the collision, and it doesn’t have to be turned into a war. An outburst is like a gust of wind that doesn’t last all day. Afterward you can return to gentleness, without punishing yourself.
anger_at_loved.practice: After an outburst, picture two boats that have bumped into each other on a river. Ask yourself: what in this situation was “current” rather than ill intent?

ambivalence.text: Loving someone and at the same time being unable to stand them — it seems it shouldn’t be this way. But for Taoism it is entirely natural. The yin-yang symbol shows it: there is always a dark dot in the light and a light dot in the dark, and they flow into each other ceaselessly. Laozi wrote that opposites give birth to one another: difficult and easy complete each other, long and short define each other (chapter 2). From a Taoist point of view, mixed feelings toward someone close aren’t a broken love but a living one: where there is a deep bond, there is also friction. Trouble begins when we demand a “pure” feeling of ourselves and wage war on its other half. You can let tenderness and irritation flow side by side, like two streams in one river.
ambivalence.practice: Think of someone close to you and name one thing about them that gladdens you and one that irritates you. Tell yourself: “Both are true.”

guilty_relief.text: Relief after someone leaves, after a breakup, or even after the death of a loved one who was ill for a long time often comes together with guilt. Taoism would treat it with great gentleness. There is a well-known story in the Zhuangzi: when Zhuangzi’s wife died, a friend found him sitting and drumming on a bowl. Zhuangzi explained that at first he had grieved like everyone, but then he saw that her life and death were part of the same transformation as the turning of the seasons (chapter 18). This story shouldn’t be read as advice not to grieve. But it shows that a mixture of different feelings at the edge of life is natural. From a Taoist point of view, relief is a breath out after long strain, not a betrayal of love. You can allow yourself both the breath out and the sorrow.
guilty_relief.practice: Take a few slow breaths out and tell yourself: “It’s all right to breathe out. Love doesn’t leave because of it.”

indifference.text: Sometimes something ought to move you, yet inside it is quiet and empty. Taoism wouldn’t be alarmed by this state. Laozi wrote that Heaven and Earth “are ruthless” (chapter 5) — not in the sense of cruelty, but in that nature doesn’t act out feelings it doesn’t have. Taoism is wary in general of “proper” feelings — of rules about how one is supposed to feel and react. From a Taoist point of view, you could say indifference is sometimes a winter season of the soul: the field is resting, the sap has gone deep. No one demands flowers in winter. This doesn’t mean you’ve become heartless; feelings can return, like spring, in their own time. For now you can stop hurrying yourself and stop pretending, and simply be honest with what is.
indifference.practice: Ask yourself: if my state were a season, which one would it be? Allow yourself today not to demand “proper” feelings of yourself.

escape.text: The wish to drop everything and run — from your job, your city, your role — is something Taoism understands very well. In legends, many Taoist sages left the capitals for the mountains, and Laozi himself, according to tradition, went off to the west, leaving his book with the keeper of a frontier pass. When Zhuangzi was offered a high post, he answered with a parable about a tortoise: better for it to drag its tail in the mud in freedom than to be kept in a precious box in a temple (chapter 17). From a Taoist point of view, the wish to escape may be the voice of your nature, cramped in a shape that isn’t yours. But Taoism also speaks of wu wei — action without forcing yourself. Sometimes leaving isn’t a leap, but a gradual freeing: less of what’s superfluous, more of what is yours. You can look for the Way right where you are, too.
escape.practice: Ask yourself: what is there too much of in me here, and what too little? Name one small thing you could remove this very week.

quote.text: Your name or your person, which is dearer? Your person or your goods, which is worth more?
quote.author: Laozi
quote.source: Tao Te Ching, 44 (trans. D. C. Lau)

forbidden_attraction.text: Attraction to someone unavailable or “the wrong person” arises by itself, and Taoism wouldn’t see anything unnatural in it: desires rise uninvited, like the wind. But Laozi drew attention to a particular property of the forbidden: when something is declared rare and unattainable, it begins to beckon more strongly. He wrote that if rare goods are not prized, there will be no thieves (chapter 3). From a Taoist point of view, you can ask: how much of my attraction is the person themselves, and how much is the pull of unavailability, an image I’ve draped over them? Taoism gives no instructions on what to do and passes no verdicts. It invites you to observe desire as you would watch a river’s current: without damming it and without rushing after it, but seeing where it is moving.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Ask yourself: if this person were available and ordinary, what would be left of the attraction? Write down the first thing that comes to mind.

social_anxiety.text: Shyness and fear of judgment make you shrink, as if under others’ eyes you had to become someone else. Taoism is remarkably gentle with this state. Laozi described the ancient sages as cautious, as if crossing a stream in winter, and hesitant, as if wary of their neighbors (chapter 15) — and there is no reproach in this: caution here looks like sensitivity. The Taoist sages in the Zhuangzi are often inconspicuous and quiet. From a Taoist point of view, you don’t have to be bright and loud; the value of pu — the uncarved block, simplicity — needs no flashy presentation. Fear of judgment feeds on our measuring ourselves against someone else’s yardstick. You can allow yourself to be quiet and to be present in the way that is natural to you.
social_anxiety.practice: Before a get-together, tell yourself: “I’m allowed to be quiet.” Choose one thing that comes naturally to you that you’ll do — listen, smile, ask a question.

uncertainty.text: Uncertainty is unsettling: you want to know what will happen. Taoism is perhaps better than any other school at living with not-knowing. The Tao in the Tao Te Ching is described as misty and indistinct, and the sage doesn’t pretend to know everything. For a Taoist the world is ceaseless transformation: misfortune grows out of good fortune, good fortune out of misfortune, and no one knows where it ends. From a Taoist point of view, uncertainty isn’t a breakdown but the ordinary weather of the Way. You can meet it not by tensing up, but with flexibility, the way a young tree meets the wind: bending, adapting, taking the next step as the road becomes clearer. You don’t have to see the whole trail — it’s enough to see where to put your foot now.
uncertainty.practice: Write: “I don’t know how things will turn out.” Then add: “And the next step is: …”. One step is enough.

waiting.text: Waiting — for an answer, for results, for news — is like standing before a closed door: there’s nothing you can do, and yet you can’t settle down. Taoism knows how to value pauses. In chapter 15 of the Tao Te Ching, Laozi asks: who can let muddy water stand still so that it becomes clear by itself? Water isn’t cleared by being stirred — only by being allowed to settle. From a Taoist point of view, waiting is a time of wu wei, non-action: not inaction, but giving up needless effort where it changes nothing. Checking your email for the tenth time is like stirring the water again. You can let events ripen at their own pace, and let yourself tend to what is growing right now: a meal, a walk, a conversation.
waiting.practice: Pour water into a clear glass and watch it settle for a minute. Imagine your waiting settling in the same way.

regret.text: Regret over what you did or didn’t do shows that it matters to you how your life has turned out. Taoism would suggest treating the past as material, not as a prison. Zhuangzi has an image: the fish trap exists to catch fish — once you’ve caught the fish, you forget the trap; the snare exists to catch rabbits — once you’ve caught the rabbit, you forget the snare (chapter 26). From a Taoist point of view, you could say a painful memory is such a trap too: its point lies in the lesson it brings. Once the lesson is caught, you can stop clutching the trap itself. Taoism doesn’t promise that everything worked out for the best, but it reminds you: life is a flow of transformations, and no moment in it is the last. The past is like yesterday’s water in a river: it was there, and the river flows on.
regret.practice: Write down in one line what lesson the situation you regret has brought. Imagine that this is the “fish,” and the rest can be set aside like an unneeded trap.

longing.text: Longing for a particular person is an aching feeling that stretches like a thread. Taoism doesn’t try to “fix” it. There is a touching story in the Zhuangzi: passing the grave of his friend and eternal sparring partner Huizi, Zhuangzi said that since Huizi had gone, he had no one left to talk with (chapter 24). Even the sage who taught how to accept change lightly missed a living companion in conversation. From a Taoist point of view, longing is a natural movement of the heart, like the turning of the seasons. You don’t have to hold on to it or chase it away; you can let it flow. The Taoists saw bonds between people as part of the common Way: what was between you has become part of your nature and lives on in how you see the world.
longing.practice: Recall one phrase or habit of this person’s that has stayed with you. Live one moment today “with them” — the way they would have done it.

world_pain.text: Pain for the world — heavy news, wars, injustice — is a sign that you feel connected with all living things. Taoism was born in an age of drawn-out wars, the Warring States period, and many pages of the Tao Te Ching are full of bitterness about violence: Laozi called weapons instruments of ill omen and wrote that even a victory should be met with mourning (chapter 31). Taoism doesn’t suggest turning away. But it reminds you of measure. Laozi spoke of the “three treasures”: compassion, frugality and humility (chapter 67). Frugality applies to your strength too. From a Taoist point of view, you can carry pain for the world without trying to hold the whole world on your shoulders. The soft overcomes the hard: quiet kindness and care for those nearby are also part of how the world heals.
world_pain.practice: Choose one small act of care for those around you today. Then give yourself half an hour of quiet without news.

rejection.text: Rejection hurts: it seems you’ve been judged “not right.” Taoism would approach this pain through the idea of the natural nature of things. Zhuangzi wrote: the duck’s legs are short, but if you lengthen them it will suffer; the crane’s legs are long, but if you shorten them it will grieve (chapter 8). Every creature is good in its own measure, and forcing it to fit someone else’s means maiming it. From a Taoist point of view, another person’s “no” often says that your natures didn’t match, not that something is wrong with you. A duck is no worse than a crane — they are simply different. You can live through rejection as the pain of a mismatch, without turning it into a verdict on yourself. Your shape isn’t a mistake; it is looking for its place.
rejection.practice: Finish the sentence: “In this situation I wasn’t a fit because…” — and check: is this about my worth, or about a mismatch?

abandonment.text: The fear of being abandoned grips the heart: you want to hold on to the person and get guarantees. Taoism says honestly that in a world of constant transformation there are no guarantees — but it draws not a cold conclusion from this, but a calm one. Laozi observed that whoever holds on tightly loses (chapters 29 and 64): the harder you squeeze, the more slips away. Like water in a cupped hand: clench it and it runs out; hold it gently and it stays. From a Taoist point of view, the strongest bond is one that has room in it. Taoism also speaks of the root: Laozi called returning to the root stillness (chapter 16). The root is what holds you from within: your nature, your breath, your place in the world. Leaning on it, it is easier to live through the fear that your support will be taken away.
abandonment.practice: Cup your palms as if holding water and stay like that for a minute. Then place your hands on your belly and feel your breath — your “root.”

unrequited.text: Unrequited love is one of the oldest sufferings: the feeling flows, but no current flows back. Taoism wouldn’t reproach you for it. It would remind you of ci — the gentle, caring love that Laozi named the first of his treasures. Such love resembles the Tao itself, which gives birth and nurtures without claiming or commanding (chapter 51). From a Taoist point of view, the fact that your love found no answer doesn’t make it meaningless: the capacity to love is part of your nature, and it doesn’t disappear. But Taoism also speaks of wu wei — not forcing the course of things. The other person’s feeling is their own current; it can’t be turned by force. You can let your love be, without demanding an answer, and in time it will find its own channel.
unrequited.practice: Write down what this love awakened in you — which qualities, what tenderness. These qualities remain yours, wherever the river flows.

humiliation.text: Humiliation burns: it seems you’ve been put lower than everyone. Taoism looks at high and low in an unusual way. Laozi wrote that rivers and seas rule over the streams precisely because they lie lower (chapter 66), and that water, settling in the low places people scorn, is closest to the Tao (chapter 8). From a Taoist point of view, being “below” doesn’t strip you of dignity. What’s more, Laozi pointed out that both being raised up and being humbled keep a person equally anxious, as long as they depend on someone else’s favor. Freedom lies not in regaining the “top,” but in ceasing to measure yourself by this ladder. The pain of humiliation is real, but it speaks of the other person’s action, not of your nature.
humiliation.practice: Picture water flowing downward and remaining water all the same. Tell yourself: “Wherever I end up, I remain myself.”

quote.text: Favour and disgrace would seem equally to be feared.
quote.author: Laozi

body_shame.text: Dissatisfaction with your body is often born of comparison with an ideal, and Taoism is suspicious of ideals. The Zhuangzi has many heroes with unusual bodies. Crippled Shu, whose body was so twisted that his chin was hidden against his navel, lived a long life and fed his family (chapter 4). People missing a leg or with strange looks drew others to them so strongly that those others stopped noticing their appearance: when inner power is great, form is forgotten (chapter 5). From a Taoist point of view, the body is part of nature, like a tree or a stone: it has its own shape and its own path, and it doesn’t need to be forced to fit someone else’s yardstick. You can treat it as a living, changing being, not as a project that is forever unfinished.
body_shame.practice: Place your palm on the part of your body you’re used to criticizing, and think of it as part of nature — a branch, a stone, a wave. Keep your hand there for a few breaths.

illness.text: When the body lets you down, it’s frightening and exhausting. Taoism treats the body as part of nature — with its own ebbs and flows. The Zhuangzi (chapter 6) has a striking story about Ziyu, whom illness had bent so badly that his back rose into a hump. A friend asked whether it troubled him. He answered that it didn’t — and began to wonder, with curiosity, what nature was turning him into. This isn’t a call to ignore pain, but an image of a courage that accepts change without waging war on oneself. From a Taoist point of view, the body doesn’t need to be “defeated”; you can be its companion — listen to its rhythm, conserve your strength the way water conserves its own, flowing around stones. Illness isn’t your fault or your failure, but a difficult stretch of the Way.
illness.practice: Ask your body: “What do you need right now?” — and listen for the first answer: warmth, rest, water, quiet. Give it one of these.

pride.text: Pride in something you’ve done is a good, well-earned feeling. Taoism doesn’t demand that you hide it, but it suggests a particular way of carrying it. Laozi describes the Tao as creating without claiming, accomplishing without boasting. When the sage has finished a task, they step aside — not out of false modesty, but because the work now lives its own life. From a Taoist point of view, healthy pride is like the quiet joy of a master craftsman. In the Zhuangzi, Cook Ding, having finished carving up the ox, stands with his knife in hand, looks all around him and is pleased with himself (chapter 3). He isn’t bragging — he is savoring what he has done. You can allow yourself this moment: pause, look around and be glad — without competition and without needing an audience.
pride.practice: Pause for a minute, like Cook Ding: look back at what you’ve done and allow yourself to be pleased — without judgments or comparisons.

quote.text: Retire when the task is accomplished. This is the way of heaven.
quote.author: Laozi
quote.source: Tao Te Ching, 9 (trans. D. C. Lau)

melancholy.text: Bright sadness is a quiet feeling that holds both sorrow and beauty. Taoism is perhaps closest of all to it: it sees life as ceaseless transformation, where everything comes and goes like clouds over mountains. In Chinese poetry, which grew up alongside Taoism, bright sadness is a frequent guest: autumn leaves, the moon over a river, a solitary crane. From a Taoist point of view, melancholy can be understood as the yin of the soul — the cool, quiet, inward-turned side, without which there is no yang either. There’s no need to drive it away. Zhuangzi wrote that joy and sorrow follow one another like day and night. Evening is no worse than morning — it just has a different light. You can allow yourself this evening.
melancholy.practice: Sit by a window or step outside for a few minutes and watch something slow — clouds, light, leaves. Just be with it.
